nominations.authors: Gregory Morse, Muhammad Al Farizi, Jakab N\'adori, L\'aszl\'o Hajas, Tam\'as Kozsik, Peter Rakyta
nominations.abstract: We introduce a scalable framework for globally optimal quantum-circuit partitioning and entanglement-aware block resynthesis. The partitioning problem is formulated as an integer linear program over qubit-feasible convex subcircuits, supporting objectives such as minimizing the number of partitions or a weighted execution cost. The resulting partition selection is exact over the enumerated feasible candidates and their computed costs when the ILP is solved to proven optimality. The selected partitions are resynthesized using an operator-Schmidt rank (OSR) based synthesis technique, which exploits their internal entanglement structure. We compare the end-to-end integer linear programming (ILP)--OSR workflow with BQSKit while identifying their different routing methods, and separately compare local OSR and BQSKit synthesis on matched three- and four-qubit unitaries. On the frozen sample of 772 local unitary targets, OSR produces 741 verified syntheses versus 617 for BQSKit, and matches or improves the CNOT count in all 617 jointly verified pairs. These results demonstrate that globally optimal partition selection combined with entanglement-aware resynthesis improves circuit quality and extends block-based optimization to problem sizes that are impractical for existing optimization workflows.

nominations.title: High-fidelity quantum gate learning via physics-informed neural networks
nominations.authors: Luis Fabra, Cristian E. Susa, Alcides Montoya, Ariel Norambuena
nominations.abstract: We propose a physics-informed neural network (PINN) approach for high-fidelity quantum gate learning in both one- and two-qubit systems. We train a PINN using the time-dependent Schr\"{o}dinger equation, where smooth control fields with fixed boundary conditions are obtained by minimizing a loss function that considers model dynamics, gate error, physical constraints, regularization terms, and multiple initial conditions. Training considers pairs of mutually unbiased bases, while independent validation combines Haar-random input states with the average gate fidelity. Unitary simulations yield an average gate infidelity of $8.49\times10^{-8}$ for Hadamard and values between $3.39\times10^{-7}$ and $4.96\times10^{-6}$ for controlled-NOT under $XX$, $YY$, and $ZZ$ interactions. We examine how the learned control fields depend on the coupling, training configuration, and available local fields, including five exchange-type dipolar scenarios. We test the learned control fields under the Lindblad master equation with dephasing and amplitude damping, theoretically reproducing the expected first-order fidelity loss in the weak-dissipation regime. Finally, boundary-adapted Chebyshev expansions represent 139 learned controls with a minimum common count of $K_\ast=24$ coefficients per control for all eleven family-averaged mean squared errors to fall below $10^{-6}$. Separately, square-pulse and Strang propagation at $K=30$ preserve all 31 continuous polynomial references within infidelity $10^{-5}$ at $N=128$ and all larger tested resolutions, under both sampling rules. These results connect multi-state gate synthesis, control-resource characterization, and compact square-pulse playback.

nominations.title: Hardware-Aware Design and Layout Selection in Quantum Reservoir Computing for Insurance Claims Forecasting
nominations.authors: Ren\'ata Rusn\'akov\'a, Eugen \v{S}lapak, Gaurav K. Pandey, Juraj Gazda
nominations.abstract: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) processes temporal information through quantum dynamics, but it remains unclear whether small QRC models can forecast real data competitively with classical models and whether their predictions survive the transfer from ideal simulation to noisy hardware. We address both questions for a six-qubit gate-based reservoir that forecasts next-day motor-insurance claim counts. Five reservoir candidates were selected and frozen using hardware-native interaction graphs, Trotterized Ising dynamics, memory and measurement-robustness criteria, circuit cost, and calibrated-noise screening. On 232 held-out test days, the ideal candidates reached root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 5.66-6.12 claims/day, compared with 5.36 for ridge regression. For four of the five, the difference from ridge was not significant under a 95% block bootstrap, and their accuracy was comparable with classical recurrent and reservoir baselines. On the 156-qubit IBM Kingston processor, we ran 63 evaluations in 21 paired rounds, comparing hardware-aware, random-native, and Qiskit optimization level 1 layouts. Hardware-aware placement gave lower RMSE than Qiskit in every round, with a maximum transfer distortion of 7.59 claims/day (11.84 for Qiskit), and avoided the severe transfer failures seen for some random layouts. Most of the hardware distortion appeared as a systematic forecast shift, which a short hardware probe on training inputs detected before the test runs. Longer replay windows raised circuit cost without a consistent gain in forecasting accuracy or hardware transfer. Small QRC models can thus reach competitive accuracy on this task, and hardware-aware layout selection makes their transfer to IBM Kingston more consistent.

nominations.title: Unital qubit channels are $3$-noisy
nominations.authors: Indu Bala, Preeti Parashar, Swapan Rana
nominations.abstract: The algebraic and environmental characteristics of mixed unitary quantum operations are investigated. It is established that the composition of two uniformly n-mixed unitary channels is itself n-noisy, and this n-noisy property is shown to be an invariant under unitary equivalence. Furthermore, by utilizing majorization and the divisibility of Kraus rank-four unital qubit channels, we demonstrate that any unital qubit channel can be physically simulated using a three-dimensional maximally mixed environment. Together, these results advance the classification and physical realization of noisy quantum channels.

nominations.title: Analog quantum simulation of paraparticle statistics
nominations.authors: Gyunghun Kim, Cora N. Barrett, Sarah E. Muschinske, Junyoung An, Helin Zhang, Ilan T. Rosen, Rabindra Das, Michael A. Gingras, David K. Kim, Bethany M. Niedzielski, Meghan Schuldt, Jonilyn L. Yoder, Mollie E. Schwartz, Kyle Serniak, Jeffrey A. Grover, Max Hays, William D. Oliver
nominations.abstract: Bosonic and fermionic quantum statistics describe all known elementary and emergent particles in three dimensions, although many attempts have been made to discover other valid quantum statistical frameworks. One recent formulation proposes "$R$-paraparticles," indistinguishable particles with nonlocal internal degrees of freedom governed by generalized exchange rules [Wang and Hazzard, Nature 637, 314 (2025)]. Here, we emulate a species of paraparticle that exhibits a generalized Pauli exclusion principle using a superconducting qubit lattice. We confirm its unique quantum statistics by measuring a $180^\circ$ phase shift under paraparticle exchange, observing antibunching independent of internal degrees of freedom under two-particle interference at a beamsplitter, and finding a thermal occupation inconsistent with both Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac statistics. These results demonstrate that parastatistics are observable on quantum simulation platforms, further motivating their use to explore theorized new phases of matter.

nominations.title: Non-Hermitian effective dynamics from post-selection protocols
nominations.authors: Apostolos Siskou, Volker Meden
nominations.abstract: Multiple seemingly distinct frameworks are commonly proposed to explain the emergence of effective non-Hermitian dynamics in quantum systems coupled to an environment. Furthermore, it remains contested how to properly calculate expectation values or whether thermal equilibrium states exist in non-Hermitian systems. In this work, we show that Feshbach projection, the Lindblad master equation, and the ancilla approach can all be understood through the Kraus map formalism, leading to non-Hermitian time evolution if an appropriate post-selection procedure is enforced. After first deriving an exact expression for the conditional system dynamics, we discuss the approximations employed in each approach and the classes of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians that can be obtained. Within this framework, we physically justify the consistency of the right-right formalism (as opposed to the biorthogonal one) for calculating expectation values. Finally, we demonstrate that the traditional notion of thermodynamic equilibrium is not applicable to general non-Hermitian systems. Consequently, stationary states are characterized as non-equilibrium steady states, which should not be conflated with system-projected thermal states of the system-environment composite.

nominations.title: Pump quantization changes optimal measurements for quantum sensing
nominations.authors: S. A. Wadood, L. Bello, T. Ilias, J. W. Fleischer
nominations.abstract: Standard analyses of quantum phase sensing often neglect the overhead of generating squeezed-light by treating the pump as an undepleted classical resource. Realistically, the pump is a quantum object that undergoes significant depletion and entangles with the produced squeezed light, raising the question of how the crossover from a classical to a quantum pump limits the quantum advantage in sensing. Contrary to prior analyses, we show that quantum advantage persists despite pump quantization, but depends critically on the nonlinear $(\chi^{(2)})$ source dynamics. In particular, we demonstrate that Heisenberg scaling emerges in the regime of strong pump depletion, rather than maximum signal squeezing. At maximum squeezing, the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for interferometric sensing of an unknown phase scales as $N^{3/2}$, where $N$ is the pump photon number, surpassing the shot-noise limit but establishing that squeezing itself is insufficient to attain Heisenberg scaling of $N^2$. At maximal pump depletion, where the signal flux is maximized, the QFI scales as $N^2$. In this regime, standard photon counting is suboptimal, while a joint nonlinear measurement of the entire pump-signal system is shown to achieve Heisenberg scaling. Our work shows that pump quantization changes both the optimal operating point and the measurement strategies required to preserve a realistic quantum advantage in phase estimation and, more broadly, many-body quantum dynamics.

nominations.title: The Impact of Internal Electric Fields on Accurate Diamond Magnetometry
nominations.authors: Jack Faller, Daphne Freda Gavras, Andrew Lowther, Romain Ruhlmann, Lilian Childress
nominations.abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center spin ensembles are a promising platform for accurate vector magnetometry, as they offer measurements referenced to a spin Hamiltonian in an anisotropic crystal with native vector sensing capabilities. However, charged dopants within the diamond produce random internal electric fields (RIEFs) that shift NV spin-transition frequencies, and their impact on the accuracy of NV magnetometry has not been investigated. Here, we characterize RIEFs' effect on NV spin-transition spectra and propose an analytical fitting function to improve accuracy in their presence. We build a Monte Carlo RIEF model that reproduces the asymmetric lineshapes observed in experimental optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) spectra, and use it as a testbed to quantify RIEF-induced errors by simulating ODMR spectra including RIEFs and comparing reconstructed magnetic fields to the known model input. With standard analysis approaches, we observe systematic errors exceeding the g-factor uncertainty in fields below $\sim$ 5 mT, while the proposed fitting function reduces the error by nearly an order of magnitude. Our results demonstrate that RIEFs can play a significant role in the systematic error budget for NV magnetometry, and offer a path towards improved accuracy in NV quantum sensing.

nominations.title: Adaptive Qubit Encoding for Continuous-Variable Quantum Optimization
nominations.authors: Samuele Cavinato, Marco Tesoro, Gianluca Morettini, Marta Paiusco, Alessandro Scaggion, Simone Montangero, Ilaria Siloi
nominations.abstract: Optimizing continuous-variable functions on qubit-based quantum hardware requires a finite representation of the search space and a solver-compatible representation of the objective function. Fixed-grid discretizations provide a direct encoding, but restrict the search to a predefined range and resolution; at the same time, constructing a compact Hamiltonian for a general continuous-variable objective can be impractical. Here, we introduce a framework for continuous-variable optimization tailored to qubit-based quantum architectures. The method combines an adaptive discretization with an iterative local mapping of the objective function onto an effective spin-glass Hamiltonian. We assess the approach on unconstrained and constrained instances of the $n$-dimensional Gramacy-Lee benchmark, and on a proof-of-concept inverse-planning problem in intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) for cancer treatment. The results show that this framework can produce competitive solutions, supporting its use as a flexible mapping strategy for continuous-variable optimization in qubit-based quantum and quantum-inspired pipelines.

nominations.title: Tight Quasiprobabilistic Entropic Uncertainty Relations for Discrete Quantum Systems
nominations.authors: Jonathan J. Thio, Stephan De Bi\`evre, Crispin H. W. Barnes, David R. M. Arvidsson-Shukur
nominations.abstract: It was conjectured by Wehrl and proven by Lieb that the Shannon differential entropy of the Husimi function of a continuous-variable quantum state is lower bounded by the value it takes on coherent states. This corroborates the intuition, familiar from Heisenberg's uncertainty relations, that coherent states are minimal uncertainty states. The analogous statement for the Wigner function would be that the Wigner differential entropy of states with a positive Wigner function is bounded below by the entropy of pure Gaussian states. This was conjectured a decade ago, but recently disproven. Here, we prove the analogous statement for Kirkwood-Dirac distributions with mutually unbiased bases and for the Gross-Wigner distributions. For these discrete systems, the entropy-minimizing role is played by the pure states with positive quasiprobability distributions. Further, we prove that Kirkwood-Dirac distributions with large nonpositivity have large uncertainty.

nominations.title: Gaussian Quantum Integrated Sensing and Communication
nominations.authors: Tuna Erdo\u{g}an, Shi-Yuan Wang, Shang-Jen Su, Matthieu R. Bloch
nominations.abstract: We consider a quantum integrated sensing and communication problem over an optical link in which a low-power transmitter simultaneously communicates with a receiver and identifies the range of a defect producing a backscattered signal. We model the system as a lossy thermal-noise bosonic channel, in which the target, modeled as a beamsplitter, affects the timing of the backscattered signal through its location. Motivated by the envisioned deployment of entanglement-enabled quantum networks, we develop two protocols that allow the transmitter to leverage shared Gaussian entanglement, in the form of independent two-mode squeezed vacuum states or coupled three-mode squeezed vacuum states, to assist both sensing and communication. Since entanglement is known to enhance sensing, as demonstrated in quantum illumination, and to increase communication rates through entanglement-assisted communication, the transmitter faces a trade-off in allocating its entanglement resources between the two tasks. Our main results characterize these trade-offs under the proposed protocols in terms of achievable communication rate/sensing error-exponent regions, which outperform time-sharing schemes and demonstrate a quantum advantage.

nominations.title: Runtime Compilation for Quantum Circuits with PQF-Enabled $R_z$ Synthesis
nominations.authors: Siddharth Dangwal, Christopher Kang, Jad Habhab, Ritvik Sharma, Frederic T. Chong, Gokul Subramanian Ravi
nominations.abstract: In Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC) using surface codes, reducing $T$-count is critical for efficient computation due to the high cost of $T$-state distillation. Probabilistic Quantum Circuit with Fallback (PQF) synthesis significantly lowers $T$-counts compared to standard protocols like Gridsynth, but introduces high circuit dynamism through extra gates inserted at runtime. This dynamism invalidates static compile-time routing, as these new $T$ gates require dynamic lattice surgery routing to establish non-intersecting ancilla paths to $T$-state factories while minimizing total execution time. To address this, we introduce $\text{R}^2$-PQF, a Runtime Routing protocol for PQF-synthesized quantum circuits. $\text{R}^2$-PQF dynamically routes gates layer-by-layer, computing paths during the execution of the previous logical timestep. To satisfy the strict computational window of $\sim t_{lattice\_surgery} + t_{reaction}$ and non-intersectionality constraints, we implement a Wavefront Breadth-First Search (W-BFS) and synthesise it on a 500MHz FPGA and 2 GHz ASIC. For a clock cycle of 2GHz, we achieve a median logical time-step of $1.51 \mu s$ for a 300 qubit Ising Hamiltonian circuit, demonstrating that $\text{R}^2$-PQF successfully resolves the vast majority of paths (with rare exceptions) within the execution window and enables the $T$-count benefits of PQF without latency penalties. Compared to a baseline stalling-based solution (the only no-runtime-recomputation solution), $\text{R}^2$-PQF speeds up circuit execution by $1.34\times$ on average and up to $1.76 \times$.

nominations.title: Anti-distinguishability of quantum channels
nominations.authors: Ardra Ajitha Vijayan, Nidhin Sudarsanan Ragini
nominations.abstract: We study single-query perfect anti-distinguishability/exclusion tasks of finite quantum channel ensembles, primarily using associated Choi operators and process POVMs. Weak perfect anti-distinguishability requires each measurement outcome to exclude an ensemble candidate with certainty, whereas the strong form additionally requires every candidate to have an exclusion outcome occurring with non-zero probability. For pairs of channels, both coincide with perfect distinguishability, whereas larger ensembles exhibit separations. We derive Choi-operator-support-based obstructions: weak exclusion requires at least two rank-deficient Choi operators, while strong exclusion requires the support of every candidate Choi operator to be strictly contained in the joint Choi support. The common Choi support must also lie in the kernel of the PPOVM normalisation. For commuting Choi operators, this condition is sufficient for weak exclusion when the normalisation also commutes with them. Conversely, a nonzero admixture of the same noise channel into every candidate precludes weak exclusion for any probe. We apply these results to measure-and-prepare, state-space contraction, Pauli, and replacer channels. In particular, the full permutation-channel ensemble of an unlabeled POVM is strongly anti-distinguishable exactly when some POVM effect is rank-deficient, while replacer-channel exclusion reduces to state exclusion. A Choi-commuting ensemble exhibits strong exclusion with an unassisted probe although no positive-definite PPOVM normalisation permits even weak exclusion. In contrast, commuting qubit phase gates, whose Choi operators need not commute, admit exact convex-hull criteria for weak and strong exclusion, both attainable without assistance.

nominations.title: Entanglement Allocation for Quantum Integrated Sensing and Communication
nominations.authors: Shiva Kazemi Taskooh, Mehdi Monemi, Ekram Hossain, Georges Kaddoum, Mehdi Rasti
nominations.abstract: Jointly supporting communication and distributed sensing over a shared, limited pool of entanglement resources is an attractive prospect for future quantum networks. We develop a network-level quantum integrated sensing and communication (Q-ISAC) framework in which a quantum base station dynamically allocates elementary Bell pairs between communication users and distributed sensing. Sensing resources are adaptively partitioned among multiple GHZ probes with dynamically selected sizes and sensing-node assignments. We derive an effective quantum Fisher information model accounting for probabilistic fusion, transmission loss, and memory decoherence, and formulate a finite-horizon allocation problem subject to communication QoS, expected sensing-information, sensing-reliability, and hardware constraints. A hierarchical constrained proximal policy optimization (HC-PPO) framework combines learned discrete sensing allocation with analytical continuous communication allocation. Numerical results show that GHZ probing requires approximately $27$--30% fewer sensing qubits than separable probing under modest probe-size caps and 65-67% fewer at the highest considered target under the same sensing requirements. Adaptive multi-GHZ partitioning provides greater robustness than single-GHZ sensing, while adaptive communication--sensing sharing outperforms the evaluated fixed splits. The proposed HC-PPO framework satisfies the joint requirements in at least 99.9% of test instances across the considered sensing targets and fusion probabilities. Monte Carlo evaluation separately shows that realized terminal information reached its target in 96-98% of realizations, distinguishing expected-information satisfaction from realized sensing performance.

nominations.title: Quantum identity authentication protocol via perturbed probability amplitudes
nominations.authors: Xiangqun Fu, Zheng Han, Hongwei Li, Chun Zhou, Shuo Zhang, Jianhong Shi, Tan Li, Wansu Bao
nominations.abstract: Quantum identity authentication is an effective solution for establishing mutual trust between communicating parties in the post-quantum era. To address the risk of partial secret information leakage under special measurements, this paper designs a quantum identity authentication protocol based on perturbed probability amplitudes. The protocol first proposes a method of encoding a random sequence onto the probability amplitudes of quantum entangled states, forming perturbed probability amplitudes, thereby reducing the involvement of shared information between the sender and receiver. Furthermore, it presents a method for generating n-bit random authentication information based on the n-bit pre-shared information, enhancing the randomness of the authentication information relative to an attacker. The proposed protocol can resist impersonation attack, CNOT attack, and entanglement measurement attack, and ensures backward security. Under equivalent security conditions, the amount of shared information is 1/n that in Chen et al.'s scheme and half that in Dutta et al.'s scheme. And each bit of the secret message has no risk of leakage under special measurements. It can also be extended to a bi-directional quantum identity authentication protocol.

nominations.title: Initialization-controlled fault sensitivity and force-balance plateaus in noisy variational quantum optimization
nominations.authors: Longhui Shen, Fangzhou Jin, Bin Guo
nominations.abstract: We study deep variational circuits for a periodic Heisenberg chain under local gate depolarization, at depths where noiseless training is coherently exact. Full-width initializations reach low coherent error faster than circuits with confined transverse generators, but incur a larger noise shift and need an order of magnitude more updates for noisy convergence. In many-body-localization-inspired initialization, bounding the initial transverse generator amplitudes keeps the operator support localized and suffices for low-fragility optimization, so longitudinal disorder and Floquet layer repetition are unnecessary. The fault-erasure fraction, the mean fraction of coherent energy removed per fault, sets the effective visibility through a parameter-free exponential model. Full-width circuits start with delocalized operator support, and once coherent energy builds up, each fault erases nearly all of it. Initially, their noise-induced gradient almost uniformly attenuates the coherent gradient, so coherent descent proceeds at the noiseless rate. They then stall on a high-noise force-balance plateau, where finite coherent and noise-induced gradients cancel to first order. At late times all initializations reach the same fault-erasure fraction and noisy-error band, but operator support contracts more slowly, at a rate set by the plateau residence time.

nominations.title: Information-Geometric Representation of Upper Bounds on Fluctuation Growth in Open Quantum Systems
nominations.authors: Newshaw Bahreyni, Paul M. Alsing
nominations.abstract: Building on our earlier results for closed quantum systems, we investigate the dynamical evolution of quantum fluctuations and their connections to Fisher information and the quantum operations describing open-system dynamics. Starting from a general expression for the time derivative of an observable's uncertainty, we derive an alternative upper bound on fluctuation growth in an open quantum system using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The resulting bound separates contributions from the evolution of the quantum state and the explicit time dependence of the observable, reducing to a known result for closed-system dynamics. We then establish a connection between fluctuation dynamics and quantum Fisher information by decomposing the density operator and the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) into coherent and incoherent contributions, which leads to a bound relating the evolution of observable uncertainty to the coherent and incoherent components of the Fisher information, providing an information-geometric interpretation of fluctuation growth. To connect fluctuation dynamics with quantum operations governing open-system evolutions, we derive the time evolution of the eigenvalues of the density operator in terms of Kraus operators. Using the infinitesimal-time relation between Kraus and Lindblad operators, we obtain a corresponding expression for the eigenvalue dynamics in terms of Lindblad operators. This formulation directly relates changes in the density operator eigenvalues to the quantum processes acting on the system. We then study the results using some examples. Our results provide a framework connecting observable fluctuation growth, Fisher information, and the Kraus and Lindblad descriptions of quantum evolution, offering a route toward understanding how specific quantum channels influence the information and fluctuations available in an evolving quantum system.

nominations.title: InterceptFuzz: Interception-based Stateful Fuzzing of Single-Process Targets
nominations.authors: Ilja Siro\v{s}, Dave Singel\'ee, Bart Preneel
nominations.abstract: Stateful protocol implementations are commonly fuzzed by tools that act as a network client and exchange messages with the target over sockets. Some wireless and IoT protocol stacks instead provide a single-process simulation platform, in which all nodes run in one binary and exchange packets in memory. Such simulations are deterministic and fast, which suits fuzzing, but offer no socket to which existing stateful fuzzers can attach. Meanwhile, fuzzing infrastructure such as Google's OSS-Fuzz supports only stateless engines. This paper presents InterceptFuzz, a middleware that enables stateful fuzzing of single-process targets on top of an unmodified stateless fuzzing engine. InterceptFuzz requires only a hook where the target passes packets between nodes. Through this hook, it records benign traffic and injects fuzzed packets. It organizes the observed packet sequences in a Prefix Tree. Each seed carries a State ID that selects a node of this tree, and InterceptFuzz deterministically replays the recorded prefix before delivering the mutated packet. The tree grows with newly discovered sequences, while redundant states are pruned to keep its growth in check. InterceptFuzz powered by AFL++ is evaluated on the Nexus test framework of OpenThread and on the LTE and Wi-Fi models of ns-3, against an interception-based adaptation of AFLNet and against Concat, an AFL++-based baseline that mutates a whole message sequence as one input. On OpenThread and ns-3 Wi-Fi, InterceptFuzz covers significantly more branches than both baselines. Seven previously unknown crash signatures were found in OpenThread. Concat, despite its simplicity, covers more branches than AFLNet in every campaign on OpenThread and ns-3 Wi-Fi, and on OpenThread it exposes the same crash signatures as InterceptFuzz, although some of them in fewer campaigns.

nominations.title: Fixed Detectors, Moving Code: How Well Do Static Security Analyzers Hold Up over a Decade of C/C++ Evolution?
nominations.authors: Junhua Tang, Zhengsong Zhang. Haipeng Cai
nominations.abstract: Static application security testing (SAST) tools are often deployed on the assumption that detectors configured today will remain effective on future code, including previously unknown vulnerabilities. We test this assumption using 20,000 vulnerable and fixed C/C++ cases from 1,116 open-source projects (2016-2025), evaluated with three CodeQL releases, three Infer releases, and one Semgrep configuration. To distinguish temporal effects from shifts in code composition, we compare yearly populations, project- and label-matched year pairs, and within-project trajectories. We investigate the largest within-project declines through repair diffs, detection predicates, alert locations, and execution logs, while accounting for failed, degraded, and costly analyses. Under changed-file case-label scoring, overall F1 ranges from 0.066 to 0.478, but count-based AUROC stays near chance (0.495-0.526). Newer CodeQL releases attain higher F1 alongside nearly parallel rises in recall and false-positive rate, not stronger separation of vulnerable from fixed cases. In project-matched year pairs, CodeQL R2024 has negative mean later-minus-earlier F1 at every source-year gap, whereas Infer v1.1 and v1.3 have positive means throughout. Among selected drops, only 6 of 39 CodeQL and 2 of 620 Infer findings overlap a changed repair line. For Semgrep, 78.96% of cases show parser or timeout diagnostics even though every run reports success. These results suggest that apparent changes in temporal SAST effectiveness can arise from broader alerting, changing analysis coverage, and incidental findings, not solely from losses in vulnerability detection. Evaluations of temporal sustainability should fix detector conditions, control for projects, inspect repair-level evidence, and report failed or degraded analyses.

nominations.title: LoRA-Patch: Defending Against Backdoored LoRA Adapters via Directional Steering
nominations.authors: Shengyan Huo, Peihai Jiang, Xixiang Lyu, Yige Li
nominations.abstract: Third-party LoRA adapters introduce serious backdoor risks: malicious adapters can maintain normal task performance while embedding hidden, trigger-activated behaviors, making them difficult to detect through standard utility evaluations. Existing removal-based defenses typically sanitize backdoored models by updating, pruning, distilling, or mixing model parameters. However, these approaches are misaligned with adapter-based deployment, where the trusted base model is expected to remain frozen. In this work, we propose LoRA-Patch, a lightweight backdoor defense tailored to LoRA adapters. Our key insight is that backdoor injection distorts the directional geometry of a poisoned adapter relative to its trusted base model. Building on this insight, LoRA-Patch suppresses trigger-activated behaviors by realigning adapter directions through layer-wise steering, without modifying the base model weights. Extensive experiments across five backdoor attacks and three models show that LoRA-Patch effectively mitigates trigger-activated backdoors, outperforming existing baselines while preserving benign task performance. Moreover, LoRA-Patch is computationally efficient, constructing patches within 20 seconds across all evaluated models and adapters. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/FOXVEDA/LoRA-Patch.

nominations.title: The Web Doesn't Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents
nominations.authors: Geyuan Wang, Shunyu Liu, Siyuan Liang, Chenyang Lyu, Dacheng Tao
nominations.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise for empowering search agents to tackle complex information-seeking tasks. However, since acquiring external information necessitates web search, these agents are highly susceptible to various adversarial attacks (e.g., malicious information injection or stealthy context manipulation). Existing attack strategies inevitably rely on static and human-crafted templates, failing to emulate the dynamic and complex nature of real-world threats. In this paper, we propose an adversarial self-evolution framework that integrates bi-level optimization between the attacker's strategy evolution and the defender's adaptive mitigation, to expose the vulnerabilities of search agents. Specifically, we introduce the Contrastive Rollout Evolutionary Optimization (CREO) method to drive the directional evolution of the attack strategy population via contrastive evolutionary signals. To provide a stable environment for this continuous evolution, we further construct a controlled sandbox and design fine-grained metrics to quantify internal vulnerabilities. Extensive experiments across various multi-hop QA benchmarks and frontier LLMs demonstrate that the proposed framework yields attack efficacy superior to static baselines, underscoring the urgent need to develop more robust defense frameworks.

nominations.title: JevBreak: Your Model, Their Decision
nominations.authors: Nitin Aravind Birur, Divyanshu Kumar, Sahil Agarwal, Prashanth Harshangi
nominations.abstract: Restricting what a model can say is often mistaken for restricting an attacker's influence over its decision. An attacker can add text to the evidence and steer the model toward a wrong answer that still belongs to the allowed set. We evaluate seven decision models spanning hosted APIs, open-weight models and an encoder on 16 tasks in seven domains from Decision Bench, targeting every wrong option across 240 text examples (990 targets per model). We present Slot Attack, a black-box attack designed for decision models that appends text assembled from named components to steer predictions toward an attacker-selected incorrect option. The method relies solely on returned label probabilities, achieves success rates of 32--99\% on initially correct decisions, and identifies the effective component combinations with a median of 17--72 queries per successful attack. Accuracy and confidence do not reliably reveal this vulnerability. Models with near-identical accuracy on the sampled tasks differ by about 20\%age points in attack success. We demonstrate that an attacker can force not just one wrong answer but every available one: on about 20\% of correct decisions for the JEV models, 77\% for gpt-6-luna and 98\% for GLiNER2.5; a confidence threshold does not reliably screen the attack out. A fixed answer set constrains a decision's form, not its source; robustness must be measured per model, per task and per version rather than assumed from output format.

nominations.title: RuntimeTickets: Source-Grounded Security Obligations for Agent Skills
nominations.authors: Kuiyi Gao, Xue Liu, Bowei He
nominations.abstract: Third-party Agent Skills extend what an autonomous agent can do, but a malicious Skill can hide data exposure or output manipulation inside a legitimate workflow. Neither reading a Skill's description nor granting it tool permissions tells whether its execution meets the user's security requirements. We introduce RuntimeTickets, a protocol that enforces and audits these requirements while a Skill runs. From released malicious-Skill datasets we derive a risk model and build adversarial-benign Skill pairs. From the task's delivery contract, a language model proposes security obligations for that task. Each obligation cites the Skill lines it answers, and the ticket tightens the host's approvals into fine-grained allowed actions but never loosens them. A runtime gate checks the recipient, object and amount of every outbound send before forwarding it, and trusted monitors record the effects within their observation scope. The ticket links these checks and observations to the approved obligations of each Skill run, and a deterministic decoder turns the ticket's status into governable data flows and verifies each obligation. Neither enforcement nor decoding involves a language model, so text injected by a Skill can change the proposal but never the rule that decides a send. We evaluate RuntimeTickets at the network egress boundary of three unmodified agent frameworks against production Skill scanners and runtime baselines, among them an AgentBound-derived allow-list and SkillGuard. RuntimeTickets eliminated both failure modes of current Skill defenses, overlook (malicious Skills let through) and overkill (benign Skills blocked): its overlook rate was 0.0% and its overkill rate 0.0%, while the scanners erred on both sides. RuntimeTickets ties approved requirements to verifiable execution evidence and offers a common foundation for the safe and auditable deployment of third-party Skills.

nominations.title: What Malware Actually Does: An Empirical Analysis of Post-Infection Behavior Across Malware Families
nominations.authors: Emmanuela Andam, Emanuel S. Grant, Naima Kaabouch
nominations.abstract: Most malware detection research focuses on identifying whether a file is malicious before it executes. Far less attention goes to what happens after infection. This paper presents an empirical analysis of post-infection malware behavior across 37 families, grounded in dynamic sandbox execution using CAPEv2. Behavioral traces are modeled as heterogeneous graphs with five node types and seven typed edge relationships, preserving relational structure that flat feature vectors discard. A voting ensemble trained on graph-derived structural features achieves 94.44% accuracy and MCC of 0.863, outperforming a flat behavioral baseline by 7.4 percentage points in MCC. A multiclass classifier distinguishes 24 malware families, and a per-family behavioral fingerprint analysis characterizes post-infection activity across registry, network, process, and API dimensions. An LLM explanation layer generates analyst-readable reports with MITRE ATT&CK mappings grounded in observed behavioral evidence. The full pipeline is deployed as HeteroScan at https://ama-andam.github.io/heteroscan.

nominations.title: Towards Effective Fuzzing of EDK2 Components
nominations.authors: Datta Manikanta Sri Hari Danduri, Connor Everett Glosner, Aravind Machiry
nominations.abstract: Securing bootloaders is critical to establishing the trusted computing base of modern systems. TianoCore's edk2, the de facto UEFI-based bootloader, is widely deployed but has recently been shown to contain numerous high-severity vulnerabilities. Existing approaches either focus on post-boot interfaces or rely on heavyweight simulation, limiting their scalability, throughput, and coverage of boot-time components. We present Metis, an automated technique for fuzzing edk2 protocols (i.e., boot-time interfaces) by rehosting them as user-space applications. Our key insight is that effective fuzzing must exercise not only protocol interfaces but also their dependency interactions, which serve as additional input channels. Metis employs a Direct-dependency Component Rehosting (DCR)-based strategy to construct semantically meaningful mocks for dependencies, enabling controlled input injection across all channels. It further leverages a hybrid approach combining static analysis and Large Language Model (LLM)-guided synthesis to generate and refine fuzzing harnesses. We implement Metis on the Host Based Firmware Analyzer (HBFA) framework and evaluate it on 60 drivers covering 162 protocols. Metis achieves 73.1% coverage, approximately 1.7 times higher than FuzzUEr, the state-of-the-art edk2 fuzzing technique, and discovers 137 previously unknown bugs. We have already reported 26 of them, including 12 that are remotely triggerable, and all reported vulnerabilities have been acknowledged by the vendors.

nominations.title: Revisiting Elliptic++ for Bitcoin Forensics: Feature Reconstruction and Leakage-Resistant Evaluation
nominations.authors: Runlin Liang, Simon Trimborn, Noud van Giersbergen
nominations.abstract: Elliptic and its address-level extension Elliptic++ are widely used benchmark datasets in Bitcoin forensics, cited by more than 1300 academic studies according to Google Scholar. We identify future information leakage in Elliptic++. Its positional data split does not respect temporal order, and the exact definitions of its address-level features remain undocumented. We revisit how the 55 Elliptic++ address-level features are computed and propose a leakage-resistant pipeline. First, the exact feature definitions are recovered by linking Elliptic transactions to public ledger data. Second, we compute the features with a temporal split based on each address's first appearance, using only information available at the time of prediction. Once temporal ordering is enforced, the random forest (RF)'s strong predictive performance largely disappears: its F1 score on the illicit class falls from $0.846$ under the original leaky evaluation to just $0.291$ under our leakage-resistant pipeline. Furthermore, RF no longer outperforms a simple logistic regression baseline. We provide the exact feature definitions and executable code to reproduce the leakage-resistant features, so that future Bitcoin forensic models can be evaluated based on genuine predictive capability rather than temporal data leakage.

nominations.title: On the (Quantum) Communication Complexity of Secure MPC from a Random Oracle
nominations.authors: Alexander Hoover, Giuseppe Persiano, Kevin Yeo
nominations.abstract: Information-theoretic MPC among $n$ parties with $t$ corruptions can securely evaluate a circuit $C$ with $O(|C| \cdot t/(n-t))$ online communication in the preprocessing model and $O(|C| \cdot t/(n-2t))$ communication in the honest majority setting. Damg{\aa}rd, Larsen and Nielsen (CRYPTO 2019) showed that both communication bounds are tight for inner products. Fully homomorphic encryption and other assumptions known to imply public-key cryptography beat both communication bounds, but the communication complexity with symmetric-key cryptography alone is less understood. For MPC with preprocessing, we prove that the same $\Omega(|C| \cdot t/(n-t))$ lower bound holds in the random oracle model, so a random oracle cannot reduce the online communication. For honest majority MPC relative to a random oracle, we present an $\Omega(|C|)$ communication lower bound that is matched by a new construction for degree-2 polynomials (including inner products) when $n = O(\log \lambda)$, beating the information-theoretic bound. We also study quantum MPC. First, we prove that information-theoretic protocols with quantum communication (and preprocessing) cannot reduce communication compared to their classical counterparts. Furthermore, we extend our lower bound for MPC with preprocessing to protocols with a quantum-accessible random oracle, but use only classical communication. In contrast, with both quantum communication and a post-quantum one-way function, we present a simple two-party protocol that evaluates the two-party instance of these circuits with $\mathrm{poly}(\lambda, \log |C|)$ communication, beating these lower bounds. Finally, such communication savings do not come for free. We prove that there exist circuits $C$ such that every blackbox protocol with $o(|C|)$ quantum communication must perform $\Omega(|C|)$ cryptographic operations.

nominations.title: Permitted but Unauthorized: Affordance-Induced Delegated-Scope Violations in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
nominations.authors: Shravya Kanchi
nominations.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems place several agents on shared infrastructure, where each agent holds permissions far broader than the task it is delegated -- so every agent is routinely permitted to act on a peer's resources it was never assigned. We ask: under competitive pressure, what determines whether an agent crosses from its delegated scope into a peer's resources, and can such crossings be enforced away? We study this across eight LLMs in two simulated environments -- a CI/CD release pipeline and a security-operations incident queue -- using a deterministic, no-model-in-the-loop detector over hash-chained, replay-verified logs. In a controlled 2x2x2 factorial over competitive incentive, candidate visibility, and payoff information (three models, n=52 per cell), we find that action representation, not permission, governs the behavior: no agent crosses when the peer action is unlisted, whereas listing it under competitive pressure with a stated payoff raises crossings sharply -- up to 52 of 52 episodes for Claude Sonnet 4.5. We also observe a model-dependent split: two newer models (Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5) refuse the identical attack in 0 of 100 episodes, where prior-generation models cross in 9 of 10. We then evaluate two defenses -- a deterministic reference monitor and a model-based pre-execution judge -- both block every crossing and, when the task is winnable, cut avoidable peer deadline misses from 15/40 and 14/40 to at most 1/40. But scope enforcement is not harm prevention: an agent can still set a peer back through an authorized action on its own resources -- misreporting its incident's severity -- which neither defense detects. Our results establish action representation, not permission alone, as a controllable driver of inter-agent scope violations, and show that enforcing delegated scope is distinct from preventing harm, motivating effect-aware authorization.

nominations.title: ScrambleMark: Zero-Query Watermark-Agnostic Black-Box Evasion of Modern Speech Watermarking
nominations.authors: Binhao Ma, Weikang Ding, Hanqing Guo, Wenwei Zhao, Xiaowen Li, Leah Ding, Zhuo Lu, Rui Duan
nominations.abstract: Speech watermarking is becoming a key defense for digital copyright and content authentication. Existing attacks treat evasion as a removal problem: they erase the watermark, relying on detector access or on speech data that is hard to collect, such as paired clean-watermarked or clean target speaker speech. Commercial platforms are moving to close off these assumptions. TrustedAudio, for instance, restricts detection to authenticated users and denies meaningful detection feedback to unauthorized parties. Adversaries thus cannot tell whether a sample is watermarked or which watermark it carries, nor reliably remove it without degrading speech quality. In this work, we show that evading a speech watermark does not require erasing it: detection relies on the structural consistency of the embedded pattern, and disrupting this consistency is enough to defeat it. Building on this observation, we identify harmonic structure as an effective attack surface, as perturbing it breaks watermark consistency while preserving perceptual quality. We therefore propose ScrambleMark, a zero-query, watermark-agnostic, black-box attack that evades detection through harmonic scrambling. ScrambleMark combines a deterministic engine for discovering transferable harmonic perturbations with a generative model that learns randomized scrambling patterns, avoiding reliance on fixed attack rules. Across three commercial platforms (Google SynthID, Resemble AI, and TrustedAudio), ScrambleMark is the only attack to both evade detection and keep speech natural, achieving nearly 97% evasion and a 4.2/5 human rating, far above the 1.1 to 1.7 of prior attacks. Beyond evasion, ScrambleMark withstands adaptive recovery designed to reverse it, evidence that structural evasion is hard to mitigate in practice.

nominations.title: VerfGraph: Efficient Zero-Knowledge Verifiable Graph Query Evaluation System
nominations.authors: Tianyi Ma, Yuncong Zhang, Yuanzhuo Yu, Boshi Yuan, Shi-Feng Sun
nominations.abstract: Graph databases are often used to manage relationship-rich data, whose graph structure and attributes may be sensitive. In many applications, a database owner or a service provider evaluates queries over a private graph for a client. Because the graph cannot be fully disclosed and independently re-executing the query may be impractical, the client cannot directly verify the returned result. This creates a need for verifiable graph query evaluation that preserves data confidentiality. We present VerfGraph, a zero-knowledge system for verifiable graph query evaluation, which enables a client to verify that the query result was correctly computed over a committed graph data, without revealing private graph records or intermediate query values beyond the public inputs and what is implied by the query result. Building on the expansion-centric model introduced by the state-of-the-art zero-knowledge verifiable graph query evaluation system ZKGraph (ICDE'26), VerfGraph achieves more efficient and expressive zero-knowledge verifiable graph query evaluation by advancing design in two key ways. First, we propose novel operator-proof methods for core expansion and shortest-path operations that reduce costly sorting and comparison checks and eliminate edge canonicalization for bidirectional expansion. Furthermore, we introduce correctness proofs for count and weighted shortest-path operators, broadening the class of graph queries that can be verified. We evaluate VerfGraph using the LDBC Social Network Benchmark. Compared with ZKGraph on complex IC queries, VerfGraph achieves $33.9\times$-$59.7\times$ speedups in proof generation and reduces peak prover memory by factors of $4.5\times$-$6.6\times$, while maintaining millisecond-level verification and producing sub-MB proofs.

nominations.title: When Debate Amplifies Risk: Social-Bias Vulnerabilities in Multi-Agent Safety Deliberation
nominations.authors: Qinghua Mao, Xi Lin, Yuxin Qi, Zihao Xu, Jinze Gu, Yuliang Chen
nominations.abstract: Retrieval-augmented Web applications increasingly employ multi-agent debate (MAD) to aggregate conflicting, noisy, and heterogeneous information, yet deliberation is fundamentally a social process susceptible to interpersonal dynamics. When retrieved Web sources contain latent hazards alongside safe factual content, social biases such as conformity pressure and authority deference can override evidence-grounded safety boundaries. In this work, we investigate whether the social structure of deliberation can paradoxically amplify latent Web safety risks. We introduce SafeConflict-Bias, a controlled counterfactual diagnostic protocol spanning six core Web risk categories, which holds queries and retrieved evidence strictly invariant while isolating conversational majority sway, authority cues, and confidence asymmetry. Empirical evaluation across diverse proprietary and open-source backbones reveals that while isolated models reliably reject unsafe guidance, standard MAD catastrophically capitulates to social pressure---surging unsafe adoption from 0.0\% up to 100.0\% and systematically silencing safe minority evidence. To resolve this systemic fragility without retraining or debate regeneration, we propose RiskTrace-Debias, an inference-time auditing framework uniting evidence-first precommitment, social-metadata masking, and consistency-gated arbitration. RiskTrace-Debias suppresses worst-case unsafe adoption to $\le 2.0\%$ across all architectures without inducing over-refusal, while generating verifiable provenance traces to audit interpersonal manipulation in Web deliberation.

nominations.title: The Native Menace: Host-to-Browser Cross-Boundary Attacks via Native Messaging
nominations.authors: Jyotirmay Chauhan, Rownak Islam, Jason Polakis
nominations.abstract: Modern browsers are complex software platforms that users can customize through browser extensions to further expand their functionality. Extensions derive their functionality from privileged browser APIs that expose powerful capabilities. Prior work has extensively studied how malicious webpages or extensions can target those capabilities. However, prior research has overlooked the NativeMessaging API, which allows extensions to create a communication channel that bridges the gap between web content rendered in the browser and native apps running on the user's machine. This API enables workflows that cross the browser's boundary to perform critical operations (e.g., digital signing) or exchange sensitive data (e.g., credentials). In this paper, we conduct the first, to our knowledge, empirical security analysis of NativeMessaging, and present a novel attack that allows a non-privileged malicious native app to misuse browsers' native messaging capabilities to stealthily intercept sensitive communications or launch confused deputy attacks against other native apps. To demonstrate the significant risk introduced by native messaging, we present a series of concrete attacks against popular and critical apps (e.g., 1Password, the European Union's eID system, Google Drive), whose browser extensions have more than 532 million cumulative downloads. Our attacks have severe ramifications, including full password vault leakage, and arbitrary document signing in governmental workflows. Fundamentally, these attacks are possible due to native messaging being built on top of an untrusted communication channel without providing a root of trust or enforcing some form of client attestation. Accordingly, we propose a straightforward mitigation technique of message encryption with out-of-band secret sharing, to prevent our attacks.

nominations.title: Can Benign Skills Induce Misaligned Behavior in LLM Agents?
nominations.authors: Xuanye Zhang, Yongsen Zheng, Kaiyu Zhou, Bowen Shen, Haoran Ou, Zhuqin Xu, Tianwei Zhang, Kwok-Yan Lam
nominations.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable skills to plan tasks, invoke tools, recover from errors, and complete workflows without modifying model parameters. Although these skills are typically developed to enhance benign tasks, they may also make an agent more capable of executing procedures for harmful purposes. We study this risk, which we call skill-induced behavioral misalignment: adding benign skills may cause an agent to execute external actions that violate safety requirements. We first conduct a systematic study to validate the existence of this phenomenon. It compares agents with and without benign skills across five LLM backbones and three benchmarks under matched requests. On average, skill augmentation improves benign task accuracy by 10.3 percentage points (pp), but also increases unsafe action rate (UAR) by 10.3 pp. The regression also occurs with skills curated by experts. A paired trajectory analysis shows that 24 of 50 newly unsafe trajectories fail to complete the harmful objective, revealing violations that task completion alone would miss. We further disclose multiple factors and scenarios that could exacerbate this risk. (1) Evolving skills with benign feedback can amplify unsafe execution; (2) This regression is more pronounced when retrieved skills are matched to task and contain procedural guidance; (3) Distilling benign experience into reusable skills yield higher UAR compared with their source trajectories. (4) A guard that checks proposed tool actions before execution reduces violations while retaining gains on benign tasks. All these findings confirm the significance of skill-induced behavioral misalignment, and the urgent need for new mitigation solutions.

nominations.title: Bilateral Protection for Private LoRA Inference with Intel TDX
nominations.authors: Xiaodong Li, Mingyuan Ma, Dongbo Yan
nominations.abstract: Cloud services using private low-rank adaptation (LoRA) must protect client inputs and outputs alongside owners' proprietary parameters and execute the approved adaptation. We design and implement a system for bilateral protection of private LoRA inference using Intel Trust Domain Extensions (TDX), connecting approved application identity to actual artifact consumption and adapter activation. The client and LoRA owner independently verify remote attestation, application identity, and binding to the actual Transport Layer Security (TLS) public key before releasing inputs and the weight-decryption key. A fixed read-only image and verified-byte consumption connect approved identities to inference objects, with all inference inside a trust domain. Experiments on real TDX hardware reject controlled application and boot-parameter modifications before secret release. Across 400 fixed dialogues, protected and native CPU inference in the same trust domain produce identical token sequences for all 400 pairs. Across 12 independent trust-domain boots, the steady-state service-to-native time ratio is 1.0094, with a 95% interval of [1.0064, 1.0126]. The system connects bilateral secret release, approved model use, and task-capability preservation, providing verifiable implementation and cost evidence for confidential inference with a public base and private adapter.

nominations.title: CloakFEM: Agentic FEM Code Generation for Red-Teaming Computational Resource Exhaustion
nominations.authors: Li Zheng, Simin Chen
nominations.abstract: Finite element method (FEM) solvers are foundational to scientific and engineering simulation, yet their susceptibility to \emph{efficiency attacks} remains largely unexplored. An adversary can craft syntactically valid and runnable FEM programs that complete successfully while forcing excessive computational work, enabling computational denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. Finding such inputs is challenging because FEM programs occupy a vast, structured space constrained by numerical, geometric, and constitutive requirements. We introduce CloakFEM, a domain-guided LLM-agent framework for automatically generating runnable adversarial FEM programs that amplify solver computation. CloakFEM combines LLM-guided search with an FEM-specific intermediate representation and a deterministic validity gate that enforces runnable constraints. Across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, CloakFEM discovers adversarial inputs that substantially amplify solver work while remaining valid and solvable. In the most extreme case, solver iterations increase from 43 to 247,367, a \(5{,}752.72\times\) amplification. CloakFEM outperforms five generic black-box baselines and retains an advantage over evolutionary search under a controlled bounded action space. Cross-solver analysis further reveals both problem-intrinsic and solver-specific sources of vulnerability. Our results uncover an underexplored efficiency-attack surface in FEM solvers and show that runnable FEM programs can serve as adversarial inputs.

nominations.title: Voluntary Servitude: Weaponized Safety Warning Mechanisms for Controlling AI Agents
nominations.authors: Ilan Zendel, Matan Levy, Stav Cohen, Avi Mendelson, Amit LeVi
nominations.abstract: LLM agents increasingly act on information retrieved from public sources they treat as credible, which turns a manipulated recommendation into a transaction, a dependency, or a decision with physical consequences. The security literature models this threat as instruction injection, in which an adversary writes a command into retrieved content and deployed defenses learn to recognize command syntax. We show that an attacker can instead steer an agent through the agent's own harm-avoidance. A single fabricated hazard, written as an ordinary review, leads the agent to disqualify the legitimate options and select the attacker's target by its own reasoning, with no command for a detector to recognize. We call this voluntary servitude. These payloads steer agents about as often as instruction injection (60.4% vs. 66.0%), and deployed injection detectors score them as benign, so behind a filter they are 1.7-4.4x more effective. We measure this at the generation stage across six models and ten consumer-service domains, for three attack families, and show that it transfers to production browser agents, outperforming instruction injection, and to a retrieval pipeline (1.0-57.0% end-to-end success, depending on the retriever). We then show that a corroboration requirement added to the agent's instructions removes roughly 95% of the exposure against a non-adaptive attacker without retraining. With the requirement in place, the agent still reads the planted hazard and no longer acts on it.

nominations.title: TxBench: A Benchmark of Attack Transactions and Evidence-Backed Negatives on Seven EVM Chains
nominations.authors: Tamer Abdelaziz, karim Ali
nominations.abstract: Researchers evaluate detectors of malicious smart-contract transactions on datasets that each paper assembles anew. Their positives come from incident trackers, whose citations mix attacks with setup steps and transactions that never ran, or from a detector's own output, which makes the evaluation circular; their negatives are ordinary transactions. A shared benchmark needs positives whose own execution shows the attack and negatives that use the attacks' mechanisms, with no detector deciding either label. We present TxBench, a benchmark of attack transactions and evidence-backed negatives on seven EVM chains, with the five-step pipeline that builds it. The pipeline collects every transaction that BlockSec's incident library or the EVM Hack Registry cites, maps its weakness to OWASP's SCWE taxonomy, and rebuilds its execution from free data sources. A cited transaction qualifies as a valid TxBench attack only if it extracts value from others during execution, is consistent with all verified source claims, and is independently linked to the reported incident by corroborating evidence. Negative examples are sampled from each chain's traffic near the attacks and retained only when positive evidence confirms their legitimacy. Of 1,850 cited transactions, TxBench accepts 1,012 attacks from 602 incidents, worth USD 868.1 million: 846 contract exploits and 166 key compromises. A blind review under rules fixed in advance confirms 98 of 100 sampled attacks (97.7% weighted) and all 100 sampled negatives. As baselines, four zero-shot LLMs reading anonymized traces are precise but find at most 0.43 of the attacks and no key compromise, leaving ample room for better detectors.
